lesson.title: Cutoff Frequency: The Line a Filter Draws in the Sand
lesson.summary: Cutoff frequency is the specific point on a circuit's frequency response where output magnitude has fallen to the half power point, marking the edge between passing and blocking.
lesson.body:
Frequency response describes how a circuit's output magnitude and phase change as the input frequency sweeps from very low to very high, usually plotted as the magnitude of H(j omega) versus omega. Cutoff frequency picks out one particular point on that curve: it is the frequency, called omega_c or f_c, at which the magnitude has fallen to the half power point relative to the circuit's maximum magnitude, a drop of 3.01 dB, equivalent to the output amplitude falling to 1 over the square root of 2 of its peak value.

Take the simplest possible example, a resistor capacitor low pass filter with transfer function H(j omega) equals 1 over the quantity 1 plus j omega RC. Its magnitude is the magnitude of H(j omega) equals 1 over the square root of 1 plus (omega RC) squared. As omega grows, the term (omega RC) squared grows and the magnitude shrinks. Setting omega RC equal to 1 gives a magnitude of 1 over the square root of 2, precisely the half power condition. Solving omega RC equals 1 for omega gives the cutoff frequency directly: omega_c equals 1 over RC, or in Hz, f_c equals 1 over (2 pi RC).

Here is the arithmetic worked through. Let R equal 1000 ohms and C equal 0.1 microfarads, that is 0.1 times 10 to the negative 6 farads. Then RC equals 1000 times 0.1 times 10 to the negative 6, which is 1 times 10 to the negative 4 seconds. The cutoff angular frequency is omega_c equals 1 over RC equals 1 over (1 times 10 to the negative 4), which is 10,000 rad/s. Converting to Hz, f_c equals 10,000 divided by 2 pi, which is 10,000 divided by 6.28319, giving 1591.5 Hz. Check the magnitude right at this frequency: the magnitude of H(j omega_c) equals 1 over the square root of 1 plus (omega_c RC) squared equals 1 over the square root of 1 plus 1 squared equals 1 over the square root of 2, which is 0.7071. That matches the half power point exactly, confirming the formula does what it claims.

Every real filter has at least one cutoff frequency. A low pass filter has one cutoff marking the top edge of its passband, a high pass filter has one marking the bottom edge, and a band pass or band stop filter has two, one on each side. Whatever the filter shape, cutoff frequency is always the same idea borrowed from the previous chapter: the point where the response crosses the half power line.
